claims.text: The baseline system is an elemental Cr coating directly deposited on zirconium-alloy fuel cladding.
The baseline Cr coating undergoes premature failure because of elevated-temperature Cr–Zr interdiffusion.
A CrN layer can be inserted between a zirconium-alloy substrate and an elemental Cr coating.
The proposed CrN interlayer should have a thickness on the order of tens of nanometers.
The CrN interlayer will remain dense, continuous, and adherent under the stated service conditions.
The CrN interlayer will physically and chemically block mutual diffusion of Cr and Zr.
CrN has sufficiently low diffusivity at elevated temperatures to impede Cr–Zr interdiffusion.
CrN is chemically inert under the relevant elevated-temperature environments.
Impeding Cr–Zr interdiffusion will prevent harmful intermetallic compounds from forming at the coating–substrate interface.
Cr–Zr intermetallic compounds would compromise the protective integrity of the Cr coating.
Relative to the unmodified Cr-coated baseline, the CrN-modified system will exhibit significantly less Cr–Zr interdiffusion.
Reduced interdiffusion will improve coating integrity and durability during normal subcritical-water operation.
Reduced interdiffusion will improve coating integrity and durability during accident-relevant high-temperature steam exposure.
The relevant normal-operation boundary is subcritical water at approximately 300–400 °C for long durations.
The relevant accident boundary is steam at temperatures of at least 800 °C for short transient exposures.
Unmodified Cr coatings can suffer peeling and cracking during high-temperature steam oxidation.
The optimal CrN thickness and performance limits across different transients remain experimentally uncertain.
